title: Accounting Basics and Double Entry
lines: USAT-COM asks about ten Accounting questions at ICom Principles of Accounting level. In this topic expect two kinds: naming the concept behind a practice, and short transactions where you pick the account to debit or the effect on the accounting equation. Every question is solvable by hand in about a minute.
## Concepts and conventions
Accounting rests on a few basic assumptions. Learn each with one example, because questions describe a practice and ask which concept it follows.
| Concept | What it says | Typical example
| Business entity | The business is separate from its owner | The owner's private house is not a business asset
| Going concern | The business will continue for the foreseeable future | Fixed assets shown at cost less depreciation, not at break-up value
| Money measurement | Only items measurable in money are recorded | Staff loyalty is not recorded
| Historical cost | Assets are recorded at what they cost | Land bought for Rs 2,000,000 stays at that figure
| Dual aspect | Every transaction has two equal effects | The basis of double entry
| Realisation | Revenue is recorded when goods are delivered | A sale is not recorded when the order arrives
| Matching (accruals) | Expenses are matched with the revenue of the same period | Unpaid December wages charged in December's year
| Accounting period | Life of the business is split into periods, usually a year | Annual income statement
| Consistency | The same methods are used year after year | No switching of depreciation methods
| Prudence | Provide for all likely losses; do not anticipate gains | Stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value
| Materiality | Trivial items need not be treated strictly | A Rs 400 stapler written off at once
| Objectivity | Records rest on verifiable evidence | Entries supported by invoices and receipts
! Prudence and matching are the two most often confused. Prudence is about caution with gains and losses; matching is about putting an expense in the right year.
## The accounting equation
Everything the business owns was financed either by the owner or by outsiders:
- Assets = Capital + Liabilities
- Capital = Assets − Liabilities
- Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit + Additional capital − Drawings

Every transaction keeps the equation in balance. Only four patterns are possible: an asset rises and another falls (totals unchanged); assets and liabilities rise or fall together; assets and capital rise or fall together; or one claim replaces another.
> Bilal starts a business with Rs 400,000 cash, buys furniture on credit for Rs 60,000 and withdraws Rs 15,000 for personal use.
> Cash 385,000 + Furniture 60,000 = Assets Rs 445,000
> Check: 385,000 + 60,000 = 445,000. The equation balances.
## Debit and credit rules
A debit is an entry on the left side of an account and a credit on the right. Which side increases an account depends on its type. The modern rule, remembered as DEAD CLIC, is:
| Increase with a debit | Increase with a credit
| Drawings | Liabilities
| Expenses (and losses) | Income (and gains)
| Assets | Capital
A decrease is always entered on the opposite side. So an asset falls with a credit, and a liability falls with a debit.
Many Pakistani textbooks also teach the traditional (golden) rules, which give the same answers:
- Personal accounts (people, firms, banks): debit the receiver, credit the giver.
- Real accounts (assets such as cash, furniture, goodwill): debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
- Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains): debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.
> Goods are sold on credit to Kamran for Rs 20,000.
> Kamran receives the goods: personal account, debit Kamran.
> Sales is an income: nominal account, credit Sales.
> Entry: Kamran Dr 20,000; Sales Cr 20,000.
## Owner's transactions
Because of the entity concept, anything the owner takes out is drawings, and anything he puts in is capital.
- Cash or goods taken for personal use: Drawings Dr, Cash or Purchases Cr. Goods are credited to Purchases at cost, not to Sales.
- Private bills paid from the business: Drawings Dr, Bank Cr, never an expense.
- Owner brings in an asset or pays a business debt privately: the asset or creditor Dr, Capital Cr.
> Ayesha's capital at the start was Rs 250,000. Profit Rs 60,000, drawings Rs 24,000, new capital Rs 30,000.
## Source documents
Every entry starts from a document that proves the transaction happened.
| Document | Issued by | Records
| Invoice | Seller | A credit sale (a purchase for the buyer)
| Cash memo | Seller | A cash sale
| Debit note | Buyer | Goods returned to the seller
| Credit note | Seller | Reduction of what the buyer owes
| Receipt | Person receiving money | Cash received
| Cheque counterfoil | Payer | A payment by cheque
| Pay-in slip | Depositor | Money paid into the bank

! A credit note issued to a customer reduces what he owes, so his account is credited. Do not let the word 'credit' in the document's name mislead you on the buyer's side: the buyer debits the seller.
! Drawings are a debit balance, but they are not an expense. They never appear in the profit and loss account.
## Quick check
- Can you name the concept behind writing off a Rs 400 stapler at once? (Materiality)
- Which side increases capital, and which side increases drawings?
- What is the effect on the equation of paying a creditor by cheque?
- Which document does a buyer send with returned goods?
